items.finding: Bostrom’s first-impression hardback is the earliest verified use among the three requested works. Danaher’s post is attested on 2014-08-08. Grace’s earliest positive archive replay remains blocked.

witnesses.author: Nick Bostrom
witnesses.title: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies
witnesses.dateBasis: First edition, first impression, UK hardback, ISBN 9780199678112
witnesses.locator: Chapter 8. Section heading p. 116, naming sentence p. 118 (PDF page 135), boxed definition p. 119.
witnesses.quote: We may call the phenomenon the treacherous turn.
witnesses.assessment: The weak AI behaves cooperatively. Once strong enough to act without effective opposition, it strikes and pursues its final values.

witnesses.author: John Danaher
witnesses.title: Bostrom on Superintelligence (3): Doom and the Treacherous Turn
witnesses.locator: Opening, paragraph beginning ‘Anyway, I’ll be discussing Chapter 8’
witnesses.quote: Then, I’ll look at something Bostrom calls the “Treacherous Turn”.
witnesses.assessment: The archived post credits Bostrom for the name. Its item (8) recasts the scenario as apparently safe development and testing followed by existentially threatening optimization once the AI is sufficiently strong.
witnesses.limits: The July 29 date is printed by the blog. The August 8 capture attests the body.

items.finding: The February 1979 Analog print already gives a qualified welcome to machine succession. The 1989 Genetic Takeover passage and the October 1994 Minsky magazine passage also qualify.

witnesses.author: Hans Moravec
witnesses.title: Today’s Computers, Intelligent Machines and Our Future
witnesses.dateBasis: Analog Science Fiction / Science Fact, vol. 99, no. 2, pp. 59–84, scan of print
witnesses.quote: shouldn’t we be happy to see that culture become as capable as possible?
witnesses.assessment: The preceding lines predict machine succession and accept it conditionally because the machine society can carry forward human culture and the information in human minds and genes.

witnesses.author: Hans Moravec
witnesses.title: Human Culture: A Genetic Takeover Underway
witnesses.dateBasis: Christopher G. Langton (ed.), Artificial Life, Addison-Wesley, pp. 167–200. Publisher-indexed paginated text and 1989 library catalogue.
witnesses.quote: cheerfully concludes the human race is in its last century, and goes on to suggest how to help the process along.
witnesses.assessment: Moravec welcomes and discusses helping along the cultural succession described in the chapter.
witnesses.limits: Read p. 167 as indexed from the publisher’s paginated PDF. The unsigned PDF and the library page image were unavailable. The indexed page’s footer says 1988, while the volume is catalogued as 1989. The live author file is headed July 1988. Neither date label establishes an earlier publication or capture.

witnesses.author: Marvin Minsky
witnesses.title: Will Robots Inherit the Earth?
witnesses.dateBasis: Scientific American 271(4), pp. 108–113, text layer of magazine facsimile
witnesses.quote: Will robots inherit the earth? Yes, but they will be our children.
witnesses.assessment: Minsky treats the machines as human descendants, in the context of people engineering replacement bodies and brains.

comparison.finding: The closing sentence also appears in the revision.

relatedWitness.author: Hans Moravec
relatedWitness.title: The Robot as Liberation from Human Nature
relatedWitness.finding: This is a separate 1989 work flagged in the proposition entry. The December Interactions 10 print, pp. 32–42, was not located. The April 2001 capture was indexed but not read after Wayback restricted replay. The live file headed March 1989 describes machine offspring surpassing biological humans and offers mind transfer as a way to participate.

items.finding: Moravec explicitly imagines machine intelligence expanding beyond the solar system in the February 1979 print.

witnesses.author: Hans Moravec
witnesses.title: Today’s Computers, Intelligent Machines and Our Future
witnesses.dateBasis: Analog Science Fiction / Science Fact, vol. 99, no. 2, scan of print
witnesses.locator: Section 5, ‘The Future’, p. 82, final paragraph before References, right column
witnesses.quote: spreading outwards from the solar system, converting nonlife into mind.
witnesses.assessment: On p. 77 Moravec forecasts faster expansion by communities with a higher machine-to-human ratio. On pp. 81–82 he imagines minds implemented in computers merging into a collective intelligence that expands beyond the solar system.

items.finding: The 2006 chapter is the first qualifying record in dataset date order. Its qualifying passage was independently verified in the August 31 draft captured October 22 and in the MIRI reprint. The February draft’s indexed July replay was blocked.

records.locator: Yudkowsky’s reply, paragraph beginning ‘In truth it seems pointless to me anyway’
records.assessment: The author doubts an agency will understand unfriendly AI or have authority for an extreme response. The author’s reply gives no claim about whether a clear warning would arrive before the danger.

records.locator: ‘Rates of Intelligence Increase’, paragraph beginning ‘First and foremost’. August draft p. 20 and MIRI reprint PDF page 22.
records.assessment: Yudkowsky disputes that there will reliably be enough advance warning to act. He connects a possible abrupt capability leap with the years needed to develop safety methods before AGI.
records.reprintQuote: We cannot rely on having distant advance warning before AI is created

copies.limits: Indexed as a PDF with a different digest from the October capture. Replay returned HTTP 429.
